title: What a wave knows about the wind
teaches: Waves carry energy, not water; fetch and duration, chop and swell, wave speed in deep and shallow water, and waves against a current
summary: **A wave carries energy, not water.** Each bit of water goes round a small loop as a wave passes and ends up nearly where it started.
**The motion fades with depth.** Half a wavelength down, the loops are about a twentieth the size of those at the surface, so the water below a storm is still.
**In deep water, the period sets the speed.** A wave travels about 1.56 m/s for each second of its period, so long waves outrun short ones.
**Three things cap a wind's waves.** The wind's speed, the fetch (how much open water it blows over) and the duration; whichever runs out first sets their size.
**Chop is young and swell is old.** Chop is short, steep waves still under their wind; swell is long, smooth waves that have left their storm behind.
**In shallow water, the depth sets the speed.** Where the water is shallower than a twentieth of the wavelength, a wave travels at √(g × depth), whatever its period.
**A current against the waves steepens them.** The waves shorten and grow until they break, which is why the ebb off Point Wilson can turn a fair sea into a dangerous one.
**A fast boat makes long waves.** The longest waves of its wake travel at the boat's own speed, so their period is as long as ocean swell's, and they come ashore hard.

blocks.text: On 8 January 1904 the steamer *Clallam* left Seattle for Victoria. She was a wooden passenger steamer, built the year before at Tacoma for the run across to Vancouver Island, and she called at Port Townsend on the way, where Admiralty Inlet opens into the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Past Point Wilson she turned west into the Strait, into a winter gale.

Out in the Strait she began to take on water faster than her pumps could clear it, and the water rose until it put out the fires under her boilers. Without steam she could not keep her head to the seas and lay rolling in the troughs. Her officers put the women and children into the lifeboats. The boats were swamped or overturned close to the ship, and none of the women and children in them survived. The *Clallam* herself stayed afloat into the night, taken in tow by a tug, and sank before she reached shelter. More than fifty people died.[^clallam]

The *Clallam* had come up the Sound that morning and turned the corner into a different sea. Anyone who rides the ferries knows a milder version of the same thing: a breezy day on the Seattle to Bainbridge run brings short, choppy waves with white tops, while the Port Townsend to Coupeville crossing, a few kilometres from where the Strait begins, is cancelled now and then for rough water. The wind can be the same on both. Before reading on, it is worth deciding what you would need to know about a gale to say how big its waves will get, and what is different about the Strait.

Watch a gull or a drifting log on the Sound as waves pass under it. It rises on each crest, slides a little forward, drops into the trough, slides a little back, and after a minute it is close to where it started. The wave has gone on toward the shore; the water it travelled through has not.

**A common misconception** is that waves carry water to the beach. If they did, a day of waves rolling onto Alki would pile the Sound up against the shore. What travels is the shape of the wave and the energy that holds it up. Under a passing wave each small parcel of water goes round a loop, up and forward under the crest, down and back under the trough, and comes home once each **period**, the time between one crest and the next passing a fixed post. The distance from crest to crest is the **wavelength**; the drop from crest to trough is the **height**.[^height]

The loops shrink with depth. One wavelength down they are tiny, and even half a wavelength down they are about a twentieth the size of those at the surface. In water deeper than about half a wavelength, a wave knows nothing of the bottom. A submarine a hundred metres down rides out a storm in nearly still water, and the floor of the main basin of Puget Sound, mostly more than 100 m down, never feels the Sound's own wind waves.

blocks.caption: Water parcels (dots) under a passing wave, and a bottle floating on it. The drawing is always one and a third wavelengths across; the up and down of the wave is drawn far larger than true, and shallow water deeper than true. A model of small waves (linear wave theory).
blocks.task: Bring the sea floor up until the water at the bottom starts to move

blocks.text: The bottle goes round with the water and is barely carried along.[^drift] What the wave hands on, from each parcel to the next, is energy: the wind's work, stored as water lifted against gravity and water set moving. That energy can cross an ocean. A storm off Japan can raise waves that break on the Washington coast a week or more later, delivered by water that never left the western Pacific.

In deep water a wave's speed depends on its period and on nothing else: it travels about **1.56 metres a second for each second of period**.[^dispersion] A wave's crest moves one wavelength in one period, so the wavelength is the speed times the period, which comes to 1.56 times the period squared, in metres. A 3-second chop on Lake Washington or the Sound moves at under 5 m/s, with crests 14 m apart. A 12-second swell off La Push moves at 19 m/s, about 67 km/h, with crests 225 m apart.

blocks.caption: Crest to crest in deep water, from the period alone: wavelength = 1.56 × period², in metres.

options.title: How far apart the crests are

blocks.text: Because long waves outrun short ones, a distant storm sorts its own waves. The storm makes a jumble of periods; the long ones arrive first, and the shorter ones follow over the next days. Surfers on the outer coast watch for the first long-period swell from a storm far out in the North Pacific and know that the bigger, shorter waves are coming behind it.

**Estimate.** A storm in the Gulf of Alaska, about 2,000 km from Cape Flattery, sends out a 14-second swell. Its crests travel at 1.56 × 14, about 22 m/s, but the energy of a group of waves travels at half that, about 11 m/s.[^group] 2,000 km at 11 m/s is about 180,000 seconds: two days. An 8-second swell from the same storm, its energy moving at about 6 m/s, takes nearly four.

**Out in the field.** From a ferry, a pier or a beach, pick a post or a buoy and count the seconds while eleven crests pass it: that is ten periods. On a breezy afternoon off Alki the answer is usually 20 to 30 seconds, chop of 2 or 3 seconds. On the outer coast at Rialto Beach or Kalaloch it is often 100 seconds or more, swell of 10 seconds or longer. Multiply the period by 1.56 for the speed out where the water is deep.

Wind blowing over flat water roughens it into ripples, and the ripples give the wind something to push against. The push builds them into waves, and waves bigger and longer than before take more from the wind. Three things stop that growth. The waves can run out of room: the **fetch** is the distance of open water the wind blows over, and a wave that reaches the far shore stops growing. They can run out of time: the **duration** is how long the wind has blown, and young waves need hours to grow across a long fetch. And they can catch the wind: once the longest waves travel nearly as fast as the wind itself, it can no longer add to them, and the sea is **fully developed**.[^sverdrup]

blocks.caption: The waves a steady wind raises, and the height that each of the three limits alone would allow: the lowest bar wins. Wave height here is the average height of the highest third of the waves. A model: a simple fetch-limited growth law fitted to measurements in the North Sea, as the US Army Corps of Engineers uses it.
blocks.task: Guess, then find a setting where each of the three is the limit

blocks.text: On the Sound it is nearly always the fetch. A 30-knot southerly blowing up the main basin has 40 km or so of open water to work with, and however long it blows, the waves stop at about 1.6 m (5 feet) with a period near 5 seconds. Across a 10 km reach, as a wind across the Sound has, they get under a metre and about 3 seconds. Lake Washington, long and narrow, raises the same kind of short, steep chop in a north or south gale.

The Strait of Juan de Fuca is about 150 km from Cape Flattery to Point Wilson. The same 30 knots blowing along it for twelve hours raise waves about 3 m (10 feet) high with a period of 8 seconds, twice the height for the same wind. A wind that blew for only six hours would fall short of that, at about 2 m, because the waves would not yet have grown all the way down the Strait: there, duration is the limit. To fully develop a sea under 30 knots takes about 500 km of fetch and a day of steady wind, and the waves reach about 6 m (19 feet) with an 11-second period: open-ocean waves, which the Pacific sends into the mouth of the Strait.

Waves still under the wind that is making them are **chop**, or a wind sea: short, steep, uneven, a mix of periods and directions, with whitecaps where the wind tears the crests. Once waves leave their wind behind, by outrunning the storm or by the storm moving on, the short ones die out and the long ones go on as **swell**: smooth, long-crested waves that come in at a steady beat.

blocks.caption: Fetch inside and outside. A wind along the main basin of Puget Sound (dashed green, left) has a few tens of kilometres of open water; one along the Strait of Juan de Fuca (dashed green, top) has about 150 km, and Pacific swell (blue arcs) rolls in at the mouth from storms thousands of kilometres away.

key.text: Fetch for a wind along the water

blocks.text: Puget Sound is almost all chop. It is closed off from the ocean by the Olympic Peninsula and Vancouver Island, and the waves on it are raised by the local wind over a few tens of kilometres. The western Strait is different. Swell from the open Pacific rolls in at its mouth, and a boat off Neah Bay or Sekiu can meet a long ocean swell from one direction with a steep local chop on top of it from another, two seas from two winds at once. Where crests of the two line up, waves can stand much higher than either sea alone. Farther east the swell spreads out into the widening Strait and fades, and little of it gets past Point Wilson into the Sound.

Twice a day the ebb pours out of Puget Sound through Admiralty Inlet and past Point Wilson into the Strait. In the afternoon the summer westerly blows the other way, in from the ocean, and the waves it raises in the Strait run straight into the outgoing water.

A wave meeting a current keeps its period: its crests still arrive at a buoy as often as before. But it has to make headway against moving water, so its crests bunch closer together, and the energy it carries, squeezed into shorter waves, makes them taller. Height over length is a wave's **steepness**, and once a wave's height passes about a seventh of its length the crest can no longer hold its shape and topples. Before trying it, guess how strong a current it takes.

blocks.caption: A 4-second wind sea running east into an ebb that runs west, as off Point Wilson on an afternoon westerly. Across, 100 m to scale; up and down, four times true. A model of deep-water waves on a steady current (Longuet-Higgins and Stewart, 1961).
blocks.task: Guess, then run the ebb until the waves break

blocks.text: A few knots is all it takes, and the ebb off Point Wilson often runs that fast. The result is a **tide rip**: a band of short, steep, breaking seas, often with a clear edge where the current begins, standing in the same place while the waves rush through it. Small boats plan their crossings of the eastern Strait around it, going at slack water or with the current running the same way as the waves. Lesson 11 follows the currents through the narrows, and the Columbia branch takes the same trouble to the bar at the river's mouth, where the river's outflow meets Pacific swell.

parts.title: Shallow water, and the wakes in Rich Passage

blocks.text: When a wave moves into water shallower than half its wavelength, its loops of water reach the bottom and are flattened against it. The wave slows. In water shallower than about a twentieth of its wavelength, the period no longer matters at all: **a wave in shallow water travels at the square root of g times the depth**, √(g h), where g is the 9.8 m/s² of gravity and h the depth in metres. In 1 m of water that is 3.1 m/s; in 10 m, about 10 m/s; in 100 m, 31 m/s. Every wave in shallow water, whatever its period, moves at the speed the depth allows.

blocks.caption: The same wave, now in shallower water. A longer period means a longer wave, which feels the bottom sooner.
blocks.task: Make the water shallow for the wave

blocks.text: This is what happens at every beach. As the depth falls the wave slows, its crests crowd together and its height grows, until the wave is about as high as the water is deep, and it breaks. It also explains why long waves feel the bottom long before short ones: a 3-second chop is deep-water chop anywhere deeper than 7 m, while a 14-second swell starts to feel the bottom 150 m down. Lesson 10 takes this further, to the longest wave in the Sound: the tide, whose wavelength is so long that even the deepest part of the Sound is shallow water for it.

Rich Passage is the narrow, winding channel between Bainbridge Island and the Kitsap Peninsula, through which the Seattle to Bremerton ferries run. In the late 1990s the state put fast passenger ferries on that run, travelling at over 30 knots. Owners of the beaches along the passage soon said the wakes were stripping sand and gravel from their shores and undermining bulkheads, and took the state to court. The fast boats were made to slow down through the passage, which took away most of the time they saved. Kitsap Transit spent years in the 2010s testing a hull shaped to make a small wake at speed, and since 2017 its fast ferries have run through the passage again.[^wake]

A wake did the damage, rather than a storm, because of period. A boat's wake is a set of waves its hull keeps making, and the longest of them travel along with the boat, at its speed. In deep water a wave moving at 30 knots, about 15 m/s, has a period of about 15 / 1.56, nearly 10 seconds: swell, in a passage sheltered from everything but local chop of 2 or 3 seconds. Out in the channel such waves are low and easy to miss. Reaching the shallows, they slow, steepen and come ashore with far more energy than the chop the beaches had been shaped by, every time a boat went by.

blocks.caption: Six questions on waves
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A gull sits on the open water while waves pass under it. What does it do?
choices: It rises and falls, sways forward and back, and stays nearly in the same place
It is carried along on each crest toward the shore at the speed of the waves
It stays still while the waves pass beneath it, because the water below is calm
items.why: A wave carries energy, not water. Each parcel of water, and anything floating on it, goes round a loop as the wave passes and ends up nearly where it began.

items.ask: A 30-knot wind blows for two whole days along a lake 5 km long. Why are its waves still small?
choices: The fetch is too short: the waves reach the far shore before they can grow
Two days is too short a time for any wind to raise waves of much size
Fresh water is too light for a wind to raise big waves on it
items.why: A wind's waves are capped by its speed, the fetch and the duration, whichever runs out first. On a short lake the fetch runs out within an hour or so, and more time adds nothing.

items.ask: Why is the western Strait of Juan de Fuca often far rougher than Puget Sound in the same gale?
choices: The wind has much more open water to build waves over, and Pacific swell comes in at the mouth
The Strait's water is saltier and heavier, and heavy water builds taller waves in a wind
The Strait is deeper than the Sound, and deep water makes every wave taller as it passes
items.why: The Strait gives a wind about 150 km of fetch, against a few tens of kilometres on the Sound, and it is open to swell from storms far out in the Pacific.

items.ask: Why do westerly waves become short, steep and breaking off Point Wilson on an ebb tide?
choices: The ebb runs against them, so they bunch together and grow until their crests topple
The ebb carries extra water into the Strait and raises the sea, which lifts the waves
The ebb brings cold water out of the Sound, and cold water makes the waves steeper
items.why: A wave meeting a current keeps its period but shortens, and the same energy in a shorter wave makes it taller. Past a steepness of about one in seven, it breaks.

items.ask: A long swell reaches water 10 m deep, much less than a twentieth of its wavelength. What sets its speed there?
choices: The depth: it travels at about √(9.8 × 10), roughly 10 m/s, whatever its period
Its period: it still travels about 1.56 m/s for each second of period
The wind: it slows or speeds up to match the wind blowing over the beach
items.why: In shallow water a wave's speed is √(g h). Its period stops mattering, which is why waves slow, crowd together and steepen as they come into a beach.

items.ask: Why did the wakes of fast ferries in Rich Passage wear away beaches that storm waves had not?
choices: The longest wake waves had periods near 10 seconds, like swell, and grew and came ashore hard in the shallows
The wakes stood several metres high in mid-channel, far taller than any storm wave in the passage
The ferries' propellers drew sand and gravel off the beaches as they passed close to shore
items.why: The longest waves of a wake travel at the boat's speed, so a boat at 30 knots trails waves of about 10 seconds. Low in the channel, they slow and steepen in shallow water and carry far more energy than local chop.

clallam.title: How many died
clallam.text: Accounts of the *Clallam*'s loss give slightly different totals for the dead, most of them in the mid fifties. It remains one of the worst losses of life on these waters.

height.title: Significant height
height.text: A real sea is a jumble of waves of different sizes. Forecasts and buoys give the **significant wave height**, the average of the highest third of the waves, which is close to what an experienced sailor would call the height by eye. Among a few thousand waves, one may be nearly twice the significant height.

drift.title: A slow drift
drift.text: The loops do not quite close: a parcel moves a little farther forward under the crest than it comes back under the trough, so floating things creep along in the direction the waves travel. This **Stokes drift**, named after George Stokes, who worked it out in 1847, is a few centimetres a second for ordinary waves. The wind's drag on the surface adds a little more.

dispersion.title: One formula for every depth
dispersion.text: A wave of wavelength L in water h deep travels at c = √((g L / 2π) × tanh(2π h / L)). In deep water tanh is 1, and c = √(g L / 2π), which works out to g T / 2π, or 1.56 m/s per second of period T. In shallow water tanh(x) is nearly x, and c = √(g h).

group.title: Crests and groups
group.text: Waves at sea come in groups. In deep water the group, and the energy in it, travels at half the speed of the crests: watch a group and each crest seems to appear at the back, run forward through it and die at the front. In shallow water crests and groups move together.

sverdrup.title: Forecasting surf for a landing
sverdrup.text: The first practical rules for wave height from wind speed, fetch and duration were worked out during the Second World War by Harald Sverdrup and Walter Munk at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, to forecast the surf on beaches before Allied landings, among them Normandy in June 1944. Later measurement campaigns, above all the Joint North Sea Wave Project of 1968 and 1969, refined them into laws like the one the figure uses.

wake.title: A wake as a wave
wake.text: A boat makes two sets of waves: a fan of short waves spreading out at an angle on each side, and waves across its track that follow it at its own speed. In shallow water a boat moving at close to √(g h) piles its wake up into much larger, longer waves that travel with it; fast ferries are designed to pass through that speed quickly or avoid it.
